name: Zane Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an agency driver, so I go where they send me, but mostly it's a tipper truck out of Cold Ash Quarry. I haul gravel and sand to building sites and garden centres, maybe five or six loads a day when it's busy. Tipping on a slope still makes me nervous, and I've had one load go over the side of the bay. When it's quiet, the agency just doesn't ring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a quiet week mean for you at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It means two days' pay instead of five. I live with my girlfriend Kayla in a rented terrace off Station Lane, and she works early shifts at the bakery on the high street. We've got less than a month's money put by, so a wet February is a real problem. I don't have a smartphone app for anything, just texts from the agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. At the quarry the lads would just shrug. I'm not online much, so I'd say it down the pub and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes nothing for me, and that's the problem. I'm still on the agency, still not knowing if I'm working next week. Cold Ash keeps saying they might take me on permanent, and they've said that for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking every shift the agency offers, even the Saturday ones nobody wants. I'd ask the quarry foreman straight out about going permanent before Christmas. And we'd stop eating out, which we barely do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, like always. Nothing about AI makes winter shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a bad winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last January I worked eleven days. We put the electric on the credit card and I sold my old motorbike to cover rent. If that happens again, I don't know what I'd sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anywhere else nearby that could use you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's the sugar beet factory at harvest and one haulier in the next town, but they want two years' experience. So no, not really. It's Cold Ash or a long drive to the city every day.

say: All that **AI fuss** came to nothing.
I'd say it **down the pub**, not online.
The lads at the quarry would just **shrug** and carry on.
think: Nothing changes, and that's the problem: I'm still on **agency shifts**.
Cold Ash has promised a **permanent job** for a year without delivering.
do: Take **every agency shift**, including the Saturdays nobody wants.
Ask the foreman about going **permanent before Christmas**.
Cut **eating out**, which we rarely do anyway.
feel: **Worried**, because nothing about AI makes winter shorter.
S0.quote: Nothing about AI makes winter shorter.
fieldNote: **Agency work** and winter gaps are the real threat, with or without AI.
Has already **sold his motorbike** and used a credit card for bills.
Very **few local options**: one haulier and seasonal factory work.

steps.text: Take every agency shift offered, Saturdays included
Ask the Cold Ash foreman for a permanent contract before Christmas
Stop eating out and cancel the sports channel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's office stuff, not trucks, and I'd mean it. Nobody's putting a computer in my tipper this year. Down the pub I'd be the one saying, wake me up when a robot shovels gravel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried about the agency side. If an app starts handing out the shifts instead of Sharon, my contact at the agency, I'll lose the favours Sharon does me. She knows I'll take short notice and puts me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep driving. If the agency moves to an app, I'd ask Kayla to set it up on my phone, because I wouldn't know where to start. I'd try to get the permanent job even harder, because permanent means the computer can't just drop me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and annoyed. I don't want to learn apps, I want to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does Sharon matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the agency's twenty drivers all want the same quarry shifts. Sharon gives me first call because I've never let her down. An app won't care about that, it'll just pick whoever's nearest or cheapest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try an AI tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to for the job, and only with Kayla sat next to me. I'm not against it, I just don't trust anything I don't understand. My phone's for calls and the football scores.

say: Nobody's putting a computer in my **tipper** this year.
Wake me up when a **robot shovels gravel**.
think: A **shift app** could replace Sharon, who gives me first call.
Losing **Sharon's favours** means fewer shifts in a crowded agency.
do: Keep **driving** and keep my head down.
Get Kayla to set up any **agency app** on my phone.
Push harder for a **permanent contract** so software can't drop me.
feel: **Uneasy** and **annoyed** at having to learn apps.
S1.quote: If an app starts handing out the shifts instead of Sharon, my contact at the agency, I'll lose the favours Sharon does me.
fieldNote: His exposure is the **agency booking**, not the driving itself.
Relies on a **personal relationship** that software would erase.
Resistant but practical: will use tech only with his **partner's help**.

steps.text: Keep driving tipper loads and push for a permanent Cold Ash contract
Ask Kayla to install and set up the agency's shift app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and someone should stop it. I'm not political, but that's too fast for anyone. I'd tell the lads at the quarry they need to watch out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd panic. By 2031 a robot drives the tipper, and I'm 32 with no trade, no savings and no clue about computers. Agency drivers like me go first, because the agency doesn't even have to sack us, they just stop ringing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know. I'd keep driving as long as there's work and try to save, but on agency pay there's nothing to save. Maybe I'd ask my uncle about the roofing firm he works for, because I can't see a robot on a roof soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like my stomach drops. I wouldn't have a plan and I wouldn't know who to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kayla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kayla we might have to move in with her parents. They've got a spare room in their bungalow, but her dad and me don't really get on. That's what it would come to, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come around 2031. Doesn't that give you some years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On paper, yeah. But the agency will start using fewer of us way before then, testing things, cutting shifts. Losing driving work to robots is not a cliff, it's a slow leak, and I've got nothing in the bucket.

say: It's **mad**, and someone should stop it.
The quarry lads need to **watch out**.
Two years is **too fast** for anyone to adjust.
think: By **2031** a robot drives the tipper and I've got no trade.
**Agency drivers** go first, because they just stop ringing us.
do: Keep **driving** while there's work and try to save.
Ask my uncle about **roofing work**, since robots won't be on roofs soon.
Move in with **Kayla's parents** if the money runs out.
feel: **Sick**, with no plan and nobody to ask.
S2.quote: Agency drivers like me go first, because the agency doesn't even have to sack us, they just stop ringing.
fieldNote: Sees the decline as a **slow leak**, not a cliff, starting before 2031.
Has **no plan** and no savings, which is what tips him into panic.
Only idea is his **uncle's roofing firm**, a hands-on job he thinks is safe.
Moving in with **Kayla's parents** is an unwelcome last resort.

steps.text: Keep taking agency tipper shifts while they last
Ask his uncle about labouring at the roofing firm
Lean on Kayla's wages to cover rent in quiet weeks
Move into Kayla's parents' spare room if rent can't be paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to sort out what happens to drivers. Not handouts exactly, but something. And I'd say firms shouldn't be allowed to just switch overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, eight years till the robots means I'd probably get the permanent job first and then lose it anyway. But eight years is enough to learn a trade if I stop dragging my feet. I just hate starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle about roofing properly, maybe weekends first to see if I can do heights. I'd keep driving in the week. If roofing works out, I'd switch within two or three years, before the agency starts cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad, but not as bad. There's time, it's just that I'm not good at using time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, not good at using time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean I've said I'd do my forklift ticket for three years and never booked it. If someone gave me a date and a place, I'd go. If it's up to me, I'll put it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to give you that date and place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quarry, honestly. If Cold Ash said, here's a course on Tuesday, I'd be there. It's the agency life, nobody plans anything for you.

say: The **government** needs to sort out what happens to drivers.
Firms shouldn't be able to **switch overnight**.
Drivers need **something**, even if it isn't exactly handouts.
think: I might get the **permanent job** and then lose it anyway.
Eight years is enough to **learn a trade** if I stop dragging my feet.
do: Try **weekend roofing** with my uncle to test heights.
Keep **driving in the week** for the rent.
Switch to **roofing** within two or three years if it works.
feel: **Bad but less bad**, because time helps only if he uses it.
S3.quote: I've said I'd do my forklift ticket for three years and never booked it.
fieldNote: Very honest about his **procrastination**: needs someone else to set a date.
Still expects to **lose driving work**, but sees a route out.
Wants employers, not himself, to **organise training**.

steps.text: Work weekends with his uncle's roofing crew to test heights
Keep driving weekday tipper loads for Cold Ash
Back rules that stop firms switching to robots overnight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, so nobody can complain they didn't know. I'd probably still grumble though. Down the pub it'd be, that's a problem for 2039 me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I'd be 40, and that's a long way off. I'd hope I'm permanent somewhere by then, or doing something else. The thinking AI in 2036 won't bother me, I don't do any of that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep doing what I'm doing for now. I'd finally book the forklift ticket, because more tickets means more shifts. And I'd try to put twenty quid a week aside if Cold Ash takes me on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine about the robots. Not fine about this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years from now, where do you hope to be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Permanent, with a house of our own, maybe a kid. I'd like to be the bloke who knows every site in the county. Whether that's driving or something else, I don't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if it's still agency work at 37?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've messed up. A lot of people round here do agency work their whole lives, and that scares me more than robots.

say: Ten years is **fair warning**, so nobody can complain.
Robot trucks are a **problem for 2039**, not now.
think: I'd be **40**, and I hope to be permanent or doing something else.
Thinking AI in **2036** won't touch my work.
do: Finally book the **forklift ticket** to get more shifts.
Save **twenty a week** if Cold Ash makes me permanent.
feel: **Fine** about robots, **not fine** about this winter.
S4.quote: A lot of people round here do agency work their whole lives, and that scares me more than robots.
fieldNote: With ten years, the robot worry fades and **agency insecurity** takes over.
Hopes for a **house** and a **child**, which need a permanent job.
Mood stays anxious because **winter shifts** can vanish any year.

steps.text: Keep driving tipper loads out of Cold Ash Quarry
Book and pass the forklift ticket at last
Save twenty a week once he's made permanent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no plan. What would help is somebody just telling me what course to go on and paying for it. Like an apprenticeship with a wage, where I turn up and they teach me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what agency drivers get. We're not in anybody's numbers, we just disappear. If robots come, nobody will even count us as lost jobs.

headlineQuote: Losing driving work to robots is not a cliff, it's a slow leak, and I've got nothing in the bucket.
portrait: Zane, 27, is an **agency tipper driver** at Cold Ash Quarry, still nervous tipping on slopes.
He lives with Kayla, a **bakery worker**, and a wet winter can halve his pay.
Centre-ground and practical, he avoids apps and **never uses AI**.
He relies on Sharon at the agency, and fears software that **hands out shifts** instead.
With two years' warning he **has no plan**; with ten, agency insecurity still dominates.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no plan and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** where someone picks the course and teaches him.
